issues.legal_issue: A concluded order determining possession in a criminal proceeding cannot be quashed merely because an unsuccessful party later pursues a civil suit concerning the same property.
material_facts: A magistrate made a final order finding that the appellant had been forcibly and wrongfully dispossessed and directing restoration of possession.
The respondent’s challenge to that final order was dismissed in revision.
The respondent later filed a civil suit and obtained a temporary injunction, which was vacated on appeal.
The High Court quashed the concluded criminal proceedings because the civil suit was pending.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in quashing the concluded proceedings merely because the unsuccessful party had approached the civil court; the appeal was allowed and the magistrate’s order restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, a concluded order made by a competent magistrate is not to be set aside merely because an unsuccessful party later approaches the civil court. Ram Sumer Puri Mahant v. State of U.P., [1985] 1 SCC 427, concerns not permitting parallel criminal proceedings to continue while a civil suit is pending; it does not require a concluded order to be quashed. An unsuccessful party must seek relief in the civil court.

predicates.appeal_challenges_quashing_of_concluded_: An appeal challenges a higher court’s decision to quash a concluded order from a criminal proceeding about possession.
predicates.criminal_possession_order_was_final: A competent criminal court had made a final order determining possession.
predicates.civil_suit_filed_after_possession_order: A party filed a civil suit concerning the same property after the criminal possession order was made.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges the quashing of a final criminal possession order and a civil suit was filed afterward, the later civil suit alone does not justify quashing that order.

issues.legal_issue: An order in a criminal proceeding about possession determines possession at a particular time, does not confer title to remain in possession, and does not prevent a civil court from reaching a different conclusion about possession rights.
material_facts: A magistrate found that the appellant had been forcibly and wrongfully dispossessed and ordered restoration of possession.
The dispute concerned the parties’ rights to possession of the same shop.
The respondent pursued a civil suit concerning the property.
issues.conclusion: The criminal possession order dealt only with possession at a particular time and conferred no title to remain in possession; the civil court could reach a different finding, and a party claiming a better right to possession had to seek relief there.
issues.legal_principle: Section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, provides a summary determination of the factum of possession at a particular time, not an adjudication of title or a continuing right to possession. The order is subject to the civil court’s decision, and that court has jurisdiction to reach a different finding. The unsuccessful party may seek relief through a properly constituted civil suit, including a suit for declaration and proof of a better right to possession.

predicates.criminal_possession_proceeding_determine: A criminal proceeding determines which party possessed property at a particular time.
predicates.civil_suit_seeks_property_possession_rig: A party brings a civil suit seeking a determination of rights to possession of the same property.

issues.definition: When a criminal proceeding determines possession at a particular time and a civil suit seeks possession rights over the property, the civil court may decide the parties’ better possession rights independently.
